articles.title: Astronomers Uncover "Hypersoft" X-ray Sources
articles.description: X-rays showcase some of the most unique astronomical objects in the universe. Neutron stars and black holes siphoning gas from companion stars stick out like sore thumbs at this level of radiation. However, according to a new paper by Mustafa Muhibullah and Jimmy Irwin from the University of Alabama and Rosanne Di Stefano from the Center for Astrophysics at Harvard & the Smithsonian, there appears to be another group of ultra-bright X-ray emitters that we’ve completely missed until now. They call them Hypersoft X-ray Sources (HSSs) and, according to a press release accompanying the paper, might answer two long-standing astronomical questions.

articles.title: Photonic Legos of functional 3D thin-films unlock high-performance heterogeneous photonic integration
articles.description: Photonic integrated circuits route information with optical signals instead of relying only on electrical currents. Silicon (Si) and silicon nitride (SiNx) are excellent photonic platforms for waveguides, but they cannot efficiently perform the ever-increasing tasks required for fully integrated optical systems. A heterogeneous photonic integration platform capable of interfacing different optical materials with high performance is thus an ongoing challenge for both academia and industry.

articles.title: Griffin MSI's new design must go back to the drawing board: 'Carbuncle in the park'
articles.description:
The Griffin Museum of Science and Industry is one of those buildings that just looks good from all sides and angles — graced with perfect siting, courtesy of Daniel Burnham, and a great Greek Revival design by the hand of architect Charles Atwood.

The south side of the building is the winning view, of course, with that portico and the Columbia basin shimmering in front of it.

But the museum's primary elevation along 57th Street is the one everyone sees. It's an impressive neo-classical expanse behind a park-like front yard and punctuated by a colonnaded entry porch fit for the nobles of antiquity — or today's gaggle of school kids.

It's a near-perfect view that shouldn't be spoiled. But that's exactly what the Museum of Science and Industry officials have now put themselves at risk of doing.

The museum this month released plans to construct a limestone and glass "Welcome Hall" on the building's front lawn, right smack in front of that grand entrance. And it's not a small addition either.

The new hall would be almost 30-feet tall and a whopping 458-feet — nearly three-quarters of a city block — in length: A big old wide-brimmed hat blocking the screen at the movie theater.

"The vision behind the Welcome Hall is to make the guest experience more accessible and enjoyable by creating a simpler path into the building while centering the historic facade as part of the arrival experience," the museum said in a statement.

But in doing so, the museum and its design firm RAMSA are expressing these noble goals with an ungainly and unattractive entry pavilion that visually overpowers the building's historic north entrance and its beautiful, open front lawn.

The building threatens to foul-up one of the city's great urban vistas — a remarkable blend of architecture, land, sky and history. One that looks just fine the way it is.

The whole thing should be sent back to the drawing board.

The museum and the Jackson Park green space it sits on so effortlessly came at great cost. And they belong to the public.

Built as the Palace of Fine Arts for the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, and the fair's only surviving building, the edifice was saved from utter ruin by a $5 million effort — $130 million in today's money — that restored the structure and allowed it to reopen in 1933 as the Museum of Science and Industry.

The park in front of the museum was created in 1998 when a 6-acre surface parking lot — an eyesore if there ever was one — was replaced with a 1,500-space underground parking facility, costing nearly $120 million in current-day cash.

The garage gives drivers below-ground entrance to the museum, but its design also forces those who don't arrive by car to go down into the space to buy tickets, then take an escalator up into the museum.

The glass-faced Welcome Hall would link to the museum via a 124-foot glass connection that burrows straight through the center of the building's exterior stairs.

Visitors could still enter the museum through what remains of the stairs, but it's a little tough to see that historic rise of limestone just being gouged through like that.

RAMSA's design puts a new glass wall behind the entry porch's columns and retains the existing stone wall that's behind them.

Granite floors are planned for the entry pavilion, and the building's metal arched roof would be planted with grass.

"The glass entryway and surrounding outdoor space will be free and open to everyone," the museum said. "Throughout the development of this project, Griffin MSI has been engaging with local community, accessibility and historic preservation groups and receiving feedback and support."

This is laudable. The museum and RAMSA are correct in wanting to create more free and accessible spaces and improve what is a cumbersome entry process.

But the proposed design can't be the only way to go about it.

The Permit Review Committee of the Commission on Chicago Landmarks approved the museum's plan on Sept. 10, agreeing with the assessment by the Department of Planning and Development's Historic Preservation Division that the Welcome Hall "will not have an adverse effect on the significant historical and architectural features of the landmark property."

I couldn't disagree more. The Welcome Hall is too tall and much too wide. It promises to sit there like a carbuncle in the park. And its arched grass roof makes the structure resemble a displaced section of Teletubbyland.

There's enough time, talent and cash on the table to develop something far better, given the design power of RAMSA — the late Robert A.M. Stern's successor firm — and whatever portion is left of hedge fund billionaire Ken Griffin's $124 million 2019 donation to the museum that's still burning a hole in its pockets.

RAMSA's previously announced proposed South Portico renovation plan seems to be more appropriate and less monumental in approach, according to the latest renderings.

The Welcome Hall plan doesn't have to replicate that, but the design is some early evidence that a more sensitive approach on the north side is possible.

Approval from the landmarks commission and, ultimately, the Chicago City Council would be needed for the Welcome Hall to become a reality.

But the plan doesn't deserve to get that far. The museum and city landmarks officials must rethink this thing and come up with an approach that properly honors this world-famous building and its important site.

  • Museum of Science and Industry changing name after $125M gift from Ken Griffin

articles.title: To watch and watch for: Week of Sept. 20
articles.description: The Arts & Entertainment Section congratulates everyone for surviving the first couple weeks of the fall semester. There's always more studying to come, but there's also always more media to check out! We hope that you can find some time in your busy schedules to check out these selections releasing this week. Both a movie to watch and a movie about watching, Lance Oppenheim's Primetime is a drama film inspired by To Catch a Predator , a reality TV series from the mid-2000s starring Chris Hansen. Robert Pattinson, of The Twilight Saga (2008-2012) , The Batman (2022) and The Drama (2026) fame, stars as Hansen in a thrilling reflection on the predatory nature of sting operations and the corrupting ambition to create ever more captivating spectacles at the price of human privacy. The film has garnered a lot of press for its exciting trailer , which uses split screens to play on the idea of mass media, and its negative reception by Hansen himself, who plans to take legal action against it. If you want to find out what's substantial at the center of all the controversy, check out the film when it releases Sept. 25. There are movies to watch about watching or books to read about listening. Penguin Random House's new edition of Palestinian American literary critic Edward W. Said's Musical Elaborations is set to publish Sept. 22. Famous for his works in Middle Eastern Studies such as Orientalism and The Question of Palestine , Said also wrote and taught extensively on Western music. Musical Elaborations is a collection of essays from Said's 1989 lectures at the University of California, Irvine, exploring the tension between music as " an intensely solitary and subjective experience for the performer or listener " and as " public occurrence, fully implicated in the social and cultural world ." The book uses the criticism of Theodor W. Adorno, Walter Benjamin and Paul de Man in discussion about Ludwig van Beethoven, Richard Wagner and Richard Strauss. While the great canonical musicians might've prompted solitary reflection, R&B pop artist Tinashe's new album Popstar seems to be destined for those ego-death crowded moments at the club. Coming off the success of her hit single " Nasty " on Quantum Baby (2024), Popstar will be Tinashe's eighth album. Its singles include " Crash Out ," " Too Easy " and " Pillow Fight ," all with sparse yet catchy beats to accompany and emphasize her voice. Starry-eyed, Popstar 's cover features Tinashe herself in headphones with stars across her irises. Can't wait to be starry-eyed yourself? Give the album a listen when it releases on Sept. 25. Looking to combine a love for music with an appreciation of the visual arts? The Walters Art Museum is hosting " Art / Sound / Now with Love Groove ," an event that combines the experience of the museum's galleries with live music. John Tyler, the organizer of Baltimore's Love Groove Festival , will curate the live performances for a night of food, drink, art, music and community. The event, taking place Sept. 24 from 6:00-7:30 p.m., is free and requires registration. To watch: Primetime , directed by Lance Oppenheim - Sept. 25 The Incomer , directed by Louis Paxton - Sept. 25 Heart of the Beast , directed by David Ayer - Sept. 25 Never After Dark , directed by Nebâ Afutâ Dâku - Sept. 25 The Stunt Driver , directed by Michael Dowse - Sept. 25 To read: Musical Elaborations , written by Edward W. Said - Sept. 22 Hollywood, Ending , written by John Green - Sept. 22 Bad Bad Girl , written by Gish Jen - Sept. 22 Blood Money , written by Anna Seghers - Sept. 22 Playing Wolf , written by Zuzana Ríhová - Sept. 22 To listen: Popstar , by Tinashe - Sept. 25 All My Demons Greeting Me as a Friend (The Moth Tapes) , by AURORA - Sept. 25 The Gem , by Julia Jacklin - Sept. 25 Hotel Usona , by Protomartyr - Sept. 25 Leave on a Light , by Max McNown - Sept. 25 Live events: Distinguished Artist Chamber Music Master Class Series - Sept. 21, 7:30-9:30 p.m. at the Cohen-Davison Family Theatre This event is free. articles.title: Underwater Solar Cells Capture Energy 10 Meters Below the Surface
articles.description: Nowadays, solar cells are typically found on sunny surfaces on land or aboard satellites in space. A new study suggests photovoltaics can also work below the ocean’s surface, generating useful amounts of electricity underwater even at depths of 10 meters. “With submerged solar cells, submarines or autonomous underwater vehicles could achieve far greater range and mission endurance than they do today,” says Wen-Hua Zhang , dean of Yunnan University’s school of materials and energy in Kunming, China. Many other underwater electronic devices, such as sensors, cameras, lights, and communications systems “could also benefit from longer operating periods and much broader deployment coverage in the ocean, to support a subsea Internet of Things ( IoT ) in the future,” Zhang says. More than 70 percent of Earth’s surface is covered by water, encompassing vast areas solar cells could potentially be placed. However, water strongly absorbs sunlight with long wavelengths—those greater than 630 nanometers, corresponding roughly to red and beyond to infrared, microwave, and radio wavelengths. This limits conventional solar panels, which can absorb sunlight with wavelengths ranging from roughly 400 to 1,100 nm , or from blue to infrared. To overcome this challenge, Zhang and his colleagues designed solar cells that could make full use of shorter wavelength sunlight. They fabricated perovskite solar cells that cover the spectrum of light that does filter through five to 10 meters of water, which consists mostly of blue-green 400 to 600-nm wavelengths. The scientists found that while their photovoltaic cells attained a light-to-electricity conversion efficiency of 17.08 percent under the conditions usually found on land, they achieved 34.71 percent efficiency when given the spectrum of light one would expect submerged 10 meters underwater. Most standard land-based solar panels achieve an average efficiency between 20 and 25 percent. The researchers also integrated their cells into underwater mini-robots equipped with rechargeable lithium-ion batteries, deploying them near Weizhou Island in the South China Sea. They encapsulated these cells in glass, synthetic rubber, and epoxy resin to protect them from seawater. The robots could automatically maintain a fixed depth to help the scientists see how well the cells performed at different distances underwater. At a depth of 2 meters, 115 square centimeters of these encapsulated cells could generate a modest 1,416 milliwatt-hours over two hours—roughly half the capacity of a rechargeable AA battery; at a depth of 10 meters, these cells could still generate 324 mWh of energy over two hours. The performance of these cells at 10 meters exceeded Zhang’s expectations by about three- to six-fold, he says. How long can submerged solar cells survive? Compared to conventional silicon solar panels, perovskite solar cells are cheaper, easier to make, and more efficient, making them a strong choice for underwater applications. But they also often rapidly degrade in performance under intense light and high temperatures. In contrast, the low temperatures and weak light typically found underwater could allow for more durable operation. The researchers tested this possibility with lab experiments where the new cells were subjected to the kind of light seen underwater at 10 meters. Given the minimal level of degradation the researchers saw at standard operating temperatures of 25 °C—the annual average water temperature near Weizhou Island—they estimated the cells were capable of continuously operating for roughly 5.5 years before degrading to 80 percent of their original efficiency. (In contrast, standard perovskite cells begin to deteriorate after just one year of use on land, although researchers worldwide are investigating ways to significantly extend perovskite cell lifetime .) “The submerged solar cells show application potential as a real solution for underwater energy,” Zhang says. “Massive deployment of submerged solar cells could extend photovoltaics from land and space into the ocean, addressing the urgent demand for durable offshore energy supply. Ultimately, this could support the growth of the blue economy and may open a new chapter for marine energy.” Submerged photovoltaics face a number of potential obstacles, Zhang notes. For instance, ocean currents could make it difficult to deploy these devices. Seawater corrosion and encrusting from barnacles and algae could also reduce their long-term performance. In the future, Zhang would like to see just how deep underwater solar cells can operate. He would also like to integrate them with energy storage devices to create all-in-one units to accelerate practical applications. In addition, standardized testing protocols are needed to analyze submerged photovoltaic performance; these could enable comparisons across different labs to advance the development of these devices, he notes. The scientists detailed their findings on 11 September in the journal Joule .
